Studies demonstrate the effectiveness of cognitive-behavioral treatment for generalized anxiety disorder (GAD). A

Exercise, relaxation training, mindfulness-based stress reduction, and massage therapy have demonstrated effectiveness for chronic anxiety. B

background.definition: The DSM-5 characterizes generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) as excessive anxiety and worry about multiple foci of concern that occurs most days for at least 6 months with significant disruption to daily life. Such worry-proneness is often accompanied by muscle tension, restlessness, irritability, difficulty concentrating, fatigue, and/or sleep disturbance. The DSM-5 emphasizes the cognitive component (i.e., worry-proneness), whereas the ICD-10 emphasizes somatic and autonomic symptoms.

list.listitem: One-year and lifetime prevalence rates are 2.1% and 4.1%.
Point prevalence in the primary care setting is 7.6%.
Females are twice as likely as males to be effected.
Significant economic costs are attributable to lost productivity and to high utilization of medical resources.
Quality of life and role impairments are comparable to major depressive disorder.
Patients with anxiety disorders are more likely to report greater severity of reflux symptoms and sleep disturbances.
There is no evidence to date of an association between prenatal cannabis exposure and later anxiety disorder, although evidence is quite limited and more study is needed.
GAD is moderately heritable; however, it is a nonspecific vulnerability to develop emotional disorders that is inherited, reflected in part by the personality factor neuroticism.

For vulnerable individuals, worry can become a self-perpetuating, self-reinforcing habit. Worry temporarily reduces uncertainty, increases a sense of preparedness and control, and sometimes reduces autonomic arousal. Together with the usual nonoccurence of feared events, these effects reinforce worrying.
Serotonergic, noradrenergic, glutamatergic, and gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) systems have been implicated.
Increased amygdala and insula reactivity has been implicated.

Screening for anxiety in adults is recommended by the USPSTF based on their 2023 recommendation statement, including in pregnant and postpartum persons (B recommendation). A 2022 recommendation statement does recommend screening for anxiety disorders in children and adolescents age 8 to 18 years (B recommendation).B
A brief psychosocial intervention can reduce the incidence of anxiety disorder in children of adults with anxiety disorder.B
A systematic review of 29 studies with 10,430 patients found that psychological and education interventions can have a small effect on preventing anxiety disorders in at risk patients. B
Screening for anxiety disorder is not recommended in the general population. The Refugee Health Screener, a 15 item screening test, was shown to be valid and reliable in a refugee population.C

A randomized trial with 2998 patients found that a personalized GP-led biopsychosocial intervention had a small effect on preventing new onset anxiety disorder (10.4% vs 13.1% at 18 months, p = 0.03, NNT = 36.
GAD is often comorbid with depression, substance use disorders, and other anxiety disorders. C
The GAD-2 and GAD-7 are two and seven item scales, respectively, that have demonstrated reliability, validity, and accuracy for diagnosis of GAD in the primary care setting. B

Differential.Differential_Features: Worry is focused on possibility of panic symptoms that are perceived as dangerous
Worries are more compelling; irrational intrusions occur with attempts to neutralize
Worry focused on possible illness leading to reassurance seeking or doctor avoidance
Worry focused on bungled performance and embarrassment in social situations
Self-critical rumination accompanied by mood and vegetative changes
Worry about safety accompanied by hyperarousal after traumatic event

list.listitem: Excessive anxiety/worry about numerous things for at least 6 months
Difficult to control worry
Three or more (adults) or one (children): (1) restlessness, feeling on edge; (2) easily fatigued; (3) difficulty concentrating; (4) irritability; (5) muscle tension; (6) sleep disturbance
Focus of the worry not better accounted for by another diagnosis
Clinically significant distress or impairment
Not resulting from substance use or a general medical condition (DSM 5)
Patients typically present with excessive anxiety or worry about numerous things for at least 6 months; symptoms are difficult for patient to control.
Other common symptoms include restlessness, feeling on edge; being easily fatigued; difficulty concentrating; irritability; muscle tension; and sleep disturbance.
Patients with anxiety disorders are more likely to report more severe reflux symptoms and sleep disturbance.
Comorbid depression and substance abuse are common.
Consider medical conditions, drug use/withdrawal, and medication effects that may be mistaken for GAD.
If patient is older than 35 years with no increase in stress and no personal or family history of anxiety disorder, physical causes (e.g., hyperthyroidism) are more likely.
Unfortunately, patients often fail to disclose anxiety symptoms when visiting their primary care clinician.
Diagnostic testing or imaging studies are not generally recommended unless patient has an abnormal neurologic examination or other causes of anxiety (i.e., hyperthyroidism) are suspected.
The GAD-2 and GAD-7 screeningnstruments have been validated in a primary care population ().
In a screening population (pretest probability of GAD 7%), a positive GAD-2 or GAD-7 increases likelihood of disease to 27%, and a negative screen decreases it to 1%.
If GAD is suspected based on the initial evaluation (pretest probability 50%), a positive GAD-2 or GAD-7 increases likelihood of disease to 83%, and a negative screen decreases it to 14%.
If GAD is suspected, evaluate the patient with the GAD-2 or GAD-7 risk scores (). The GAD-7 is the best test for generalized anxiety disorder.
Rule out medical conditions, drug use/withdrawal, and medication effects including caffine.
Treatment is empirical, beginning with an cognitive behavioral therapy and/or an SSRI or SNRI.

Cognitive-behavioral treatment that focuses on worry-proneness, overvaluation of worry, and dealing with uncertainty appear to be as effective as drug treatment, have lower attrition, and may be more durable in adults, children and adolescents. It is the most effective form of psychotherapy for GAD.B
An SSRI or SNRI, particularly escitalopram, duloxetine, and venlafaxine, are first-line drug therapies for GAD with a good balance of efficacy and tolerability.A
Other SNRIs and SSRIs and pregabalin are alternative drug therapies.A
Benzodiazepines and buspirone, despite FDA approval for GAD, are no longer considered first-line treatments for GAD. C .
Mindfulness-based relaxation, meditation, massage therapy, relaxation training, quitting smoking, and exercise may all be helpful for GAD.B

An SSRI or SNRI is generally considered first-line drug treatments for GAD. A systematic review of 27 randomized studies and meta-analyses found that fluoxetine was most likely to induce a remission, while sertraline was best tolerated. A Cochrane review concluded that imipramine, venlafaxine, and paroxetine were superior to placebo, with an NNT of 5.2. However, they may be less effective in older adults, as found in one study of escitalopram.

A systematic review of 87 studies with 12 different drug classes concluded that SSRI's (especially sertraline and escitalopram) were associated with high remission and low risk of adverse events and should be considered first-line pharmacotherapy.

A more recent and comprehensive network meta-analysis concluded that duloxetine, pregabalin, venlafaxine and escitalopram provided the best combination of effectiveness and tolerability in patients with GAD. Quetiapine, paroxetine, and benzodiazepines were effective but poorly tolerated.
Mirtazapine, sertraline, fluoxetine, buspirone and agomelatine were also found to be effective and well tolerated, but these findings were limited by small sample sizes
To improve tolerance of adverse effects and continuing adherence, start low (half usual starting dose), increase dose slowly, and reassure often.
Drug treatment effects among grouped data are modest (i.e., 50%-60%) relative to placebo rates, which often exceed 30%.

Benzodiazepines are no longer considered first-line drug treatment for GAD because of poor effectiveness for worry as opposed to somatic anxiety and possible deleterious effects with chronic use; they do not address or may worsen comorbid conditions such as depression or substance abuse.
Buspirone is FDA-approved for GAD, but have not been compared with antidepressants. A systematic review found that they were more effective than placebo (NNT = 4).

Discontinuation of antidepressants is associated with a higher risk of relapse (OR 3.1; 95% CI, 2.5-3.9). The summary prevalences of relapse were 36% in the patients who discontinue therapy and 16% in those continuing to take an antidepressant.

A comprehensive systematic review of both effectiveness and safety of therapy for anxiety in children condluded that CBT and SSRIs, and probably SNRIs, are all effective. However, there were few head to head comparisons, most studies were too short to evaluate the effect on suicidality, and there was increased suicidal ideation with venlafaxine.

Reduction in chronic anxiety was the largest effect of ongoing massage therapy; the effect size was comparable to a course of psychotherapy. Massage therapy may be especially helpful for the somatic manifestations of GAD.
Evidence suggests that exercise and relaxation training have demonstrated effectiveness for GAD.
There are no studies on therapeutic touch.
Studies are inadequate to draw a conclusion regarding the safety and effectiveness of the herbal supplements kava, passiflora and valerian, or of meditation.
Music can reduce anxiety in patients after an acute myocardial infarction, especially when they can choose the music.
A systematic review of 39 controlled studies of arts programs (dance, music, painting, sculpture) on anxiety and depression found a moderate reduction in anxiety and depression scores.
A systematic review found that there appears to be some benefit of exercise as a treatment for adults and children with anxiety disorders.

A network meta-analysis of 65 RCTs compared 8 different kinds of psychotherapy. They found that cognitive behavior therapy and relaxation therapy were effective. When studies at high risk of bias were excluded, relaxation therapy was no longer effective. Only CBT was more effective than treatment as usual in longer term follow-up.

A Danish RCT recruited 302 patients with anxiety disorders and 389 participants with depression. A collaborative care model, where care managers collaborated with GPs to provide treatment for patients with anxiety and depression was superior to a more traditional consultation relationship.

Thirteen studies demonstrate the effectiveness of cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) for GAD relative to usual care or waiting-list controls; however, efficacy of CBT is less clear relative to supportive counseling. A Cochrane systematic review of 25 studies with 1305 participants found that CBT was effective but that studies were heterogeneous. A Cochrane review identified 33 studies with 1806 participants, and concluded that CBT was effective for anxiety disorders in children and adolescents as well. The UK NICE guidelines also endorse it as the first-line treatment for social anxiety disorder.

CBT usually includes various components such as patient education about worry as a self-perpetuating habit, recording of worries, relaxation training, designated "worry periods," and challenging intolerance of uncertainty or overvaluation of worry.
CBT as a treatment for anxiety can be delivered by phone. An RCT enrolling 141 elderly patients found that it was effective.
A study randomized 204 patients with health anxiety to either face-to-face or Internet delivered CBT, and found that Internet delivered CBT was non-inferior and less costly.

A randomized trial in adults 60 years and older compared CBT augmented by escitalopram with CBT alone, and found possible benefit to the combination with one outcome measure (the Penn State Worry Questionnaire) but not another (Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale).
CBT is also effective for acute stress disorder in patients with anxiety due to mild traumatic brain injury.
A trial with 271 participants allowed most to choose their treatment, either CBT or cognitive analytic guided self-help. Outcomes were similar at 8 weeks and at the end of therapy (24 weeks).

Preliminary data suggest that mindfulness meditation and an emphasis on futile efforts to suppress worry may be helpful additions to CBT. An 8 week RCT set in Swedish general practices in adults with anxiety and depression, however, found no difference between patients randomized to mindfulness or control. Quitting smoking can also improve anxiety symptoms, based on a cohort study of 491 patients.

A randomized trial with 276 patients with anxiety disorder found that standard mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR) is noninferior to pharmacotherapy with escitalopram for the treatment of adults with anxiety disorders. The primary outcome measurement occurred at 8 weeks from baseline. At 6 months, the anxiety scores remained improved, despite only 52% and 28% of the escitalopram and MBSR groups, respectively, continuing their treatments.
A systematic review concluded that mindfulness-based therapies are effective at reducing anxiety in cancer patients, at least in the short term.
A Cochrane review concluded that short-term psychodynamic psychotherapies are effective for anxiety disorders.

A randomized trial studied a lay person delivered empathetic conversational phone call to 240 home-bound elders (Meals on Wheels recipients). The intervention significantly reduced anxiety, depression and loneliness.

A systematic review found that ordering tests to reassure anxious patients is not very effective. For example, ordering endoscopy for patients with dyspepsia would only prevent one outpatient visit for every 16 endoscopies, and one fewer visit for every 26 back pain patients who get imaging.
A Cochrane review found that short-term and long-term collaborative care approaches improve outcomes in patients with depression or anxiety.
A chronic course with fluctuating symptoms is common. Therefore, treatment may be recurrent over a period of years. Relapse is common following discontinuation of an SSRI or SNRI.C
Life-style changes and worry-management techniques may contribute to a better prognosis. C
Patients with both anxiety and depression are less likely to respond to treatment.B
GAD usually has a chronic course, with waxing and waning symptoms over time. Subsyndromal presentations may be as impairing but are more likely to be improved on followup.
In 40-year followup, GAD tended to disappear at about age 50 years but was replaced by undifferentiated somatization disorders.
A systematic review of 28 studies with over 5000 patients found that relapse occurred in 36% of patients when an SSRI or SNRI was discontinued, compared to 16% who continued treatment (NNH = 5).
Treatment response rates are usually in the 55% to 65% range; true remission rates are usually in the 30% to 40% range.

A meta-analysis of 37 studies concluded that there is an association between anxiety and the subsequent onset of cardiovascular disease, with some evidence to support causality based on the Hill criteria.
There is also an association between anxiety and mortality in patients with coronary disease, although not as strong as the association between depression and mortality.
Genetics may impose a range of worry-proneness; however, where one typically functions within that range may be determined by how worries are valued and managed.
The first step is to recognize that worry is a self-reinforcing, maladaptive habit rather than true problem-solving or safety-seeking.
Make healthy life-style changes (e.g., regular exercise, massage, sleep hygiene,reduce or eliminate caffeine intake).

Strive to notice but not actively indulge worries. Learn mindfulness meditation to help one stay in the moment and to take thoughts less seriously. Learn relaxation exercises to help ease bodily tension.
GAD is the most common anxiety disorder among individuals >60 years of age.

Both CBT and sertraline result in significant improvement in chronic anxiety among older adults, but sertraline is particularly helpful for worry-proneness and demonstrated larger effect sizes than CBT both posttreatment and at 3-month followup.
An RCT in 95 elderly patients with depression found that the addition of methylphenidate (mean dose 16 mg) to citalopram was more effective than citalopram alone.

a systematic review of 80 studies (10 with data for pooling) concluded that data on managing anxiety in residents of long-term care facilities are limited to poor-quality studies but suggest that medications, music, and massage are effective.
Rates of both generalized anxiety disorder and obsessive-complusive disorder are greater in postpartum women than in the general population.
A small trial found a benefit to CBT in pregnant women with anxiety.
A systematic review of 17 RCTs found that digital health interventions are moderately effective for post-partum anxiety symptoms (standardized mean difference -0.49).
CBT and SSRIs are also considered first-line treatments for children with GAD.
A systematic review of 10 RCTs of drug therapy for anxiety disorder in children concluded that they were effective but also associated with a higher risk of adverse events.
Clinical trials are limited. One found that fluvoxamine was safe and effective in a group of children 6 to 17 years of age with severe anxiety disorder.

Perhaps the best study is a randomized trial comparing paroxetine, CBT, both, or neither in children age 7 to 17 years with anxiety disorders. All were effective. A Cochrane review concluded that sertraline is another treatment option for children and adolescents.

A Cochrane systematic review concluded based on 22 short-term studies in children and adolescents that pharmacotherapy was generally safe and effective. A second Cochrane systematic review also found support for the effective of CBT in childhood anxiety disorders.

A comprehensive systematic review of both effectiveness and safety of treatment of anxiety in children concluded that CBT and SSRIs, and probably SNRIs, are all effective. However, there were few head to head comparisons, most studies were too short to evaluate the effect on suicidality, and there was increased suicidal ideation with venlafaxine.

feature.caption: GAD-7 for Screening of Generalized Anxiety Disorder.
feature.feature_body:
Over the Last 2 Weeks, How Often Have You Been Bothered by the Following Problems? Not at All Several Days More Than Half the Days Nearly Every Day
Feeling nervous, anxious, or on edge 0 1 2 3
Not being able to stop or control worrying 0 1 2 3
Worrying too much about different things 0 1 2 3
Having trouble relaxing 0 1 2 3
Being so restless that it is hard to sit still 0 1 2 3
Becoming easily annoyed or irritable 0 1 2 3
Feeling afraid as if something awful might happen 0 1 2 3
Total Score _____ = Add Columns ____ + ____ + ____
GAD-2: First two items with total score cut-point of 3 or greater (sensitivity = 86; specificity = 83).GAD-7: All seven items with total score cut-point of 10 or greater (sensitivity = 89; specificity = 82).
